     design allows you to conclude and what it does not, and where the work
     goes next. -->

Habitat was recorded for the same plots as the trees, so the differences
reported here are associations, not effects: a habitat may stand for soil,
drainage or disturbance history that were not measured. The plots are also
unevenly spread among habitats, and the habitats with few plots are compared
with little power.

Distance-based methods summarise the assemblage, not its species: they say
that composition changes, not which species drive the change, which models
fitted to the abundance of each species would add [@Warton2012]. What
shapes those abundances is seen in the life of single species: on the same
island, the seedlings of *Platypodium elegans* Vogel survive better far from
their parent tree, where the fungal pathogens it shelters are rarer
[@Augspurger1983]. And the data
are a single census of 1982 of the larger trees only: the full and updated
censuses of the plot are the place to go beyond this example.
